en: Oṃ!
Victorious is service to the true guru!
Auspiciousness to the Lord of the Assembly of Consciousness!
The Thousand-Name Hymn of Śrī Naṭeśa. Preliminary Section.
Since this entire world, including all that is moving and unmoving, has arisen from him, salutations to that Naṭeśa, the embodiment of compassion.

Oṃ. Having bowed with supreme joy to Śaṅkara, the embodiment of compassion, who is seated upon a jeweled lion-throne on the delightful peak of Kailāsa, the Supreme Goddess, bowing low with humility, questioned him: "O Blessed One, O Bhava, O Omniscient One, O Imperishable Remover of the Suffering of Existence! O Lord, I have heard from you the entire *Sahasranāma* [of Śiva]. But, O Master, I have not yet heard the names of Naṭeśa."
"Though you were requested many times, you did not speak of that. Now, O Śambhu, out of compassion, tell it for the fulfillment of my desire. (4) Śrī Śiva said:
"Excellent, excellent, O Great Goddess! You have asked what is beneficial for the entire world. Formerly, the glorious Nārāyaṇa, who is devoted to the protection of the worlds... (5)
In the Ocean of Milk, for a very long time, Acyuta dwelt meditating upon me with one-pointed mind, while I bore the form of Śiva accompanied by Ambā.
6 Satisfied by his austerity and moved by compassion, I became gracious. Rising from my meditation, Viṣṇu worshipped me along with Lakṣmī.
7 He praised me with various hymns consistent with the Vedas and Vedāntas. "Choose a boon, O child, whatever is desired in your heart. 8

"I shall give that to you before long," he said; thus addressed, the lotus-eyed one spoke to me with supreme devotion: "O Lord, if you will grant me a boon—for the protection of all the worlds, for the destruction of the asuras, and for the sake of attaining complete mastery over yoga—then instruct me in a single mantra. O Mother, having been thus entreated by Mādhava, I meditated upon an unsurpassed hymn that bestows all perfections upon everyone.
I recited the *Nāṭeśa-nāmasāhasra* to Viṣṇu; by means of it, he conquered all the asuras and protected the entire world.
(12) Furthermore, the lotus-eyed one attained the perfection of yoga through his identity with the Universal Self (*sārvātmya-yoga*). O Mother, you now seek that very same *Nāmasāhasra*.
(13) By reciting and reflecting upon it, the Lord reveals his dance to one—a dance that removes all sins, is meritorious, and provides protection for all human beings. (14)

O Goddess, listen as I shall proclaim the supreme Thousand Names (Nāmasāhasra), which bestows all sovereignty, grants all perfections (siddhis), and confers ultimate liberation. Thus ends the introductory section. The *Śrī Naṭeśa Sahasranāma Stotra*.

Oṃ. Of this great mantra, the *Śrī-naṭeśa-sahasranāmastotra*, Sadāśiva is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the Mahāvirāṭ is the meter (*chandas*), and the venerable Naṭeśa is the deity (*devatā*). The seed-syllable (*bīja*), power (*śakti*), and pin (*kīlaka*), as well as the ritual placements on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and hands (*karanyāsa*), are the same as for the Cintāmaṇi mantra. [The Meditation] (*Dhyānam*):

One should meditate upon the Lord who possesses the luster of ten million suns, who has three eyes, and who bears the moon and the Gaṅgā; whose left foot is placed upon the right leg and is slightly bent, and who is clothed in a tiger skin; who holds fire, a staff, and the gesture of fearlessness in his [right] hands, and a *ḍamaru* drum in his left hand. One should worship the Goddess Śivā, who is dark-complexioned, holding a white lotus, a rosary, and a water-pot, with her hand resting on her hip. I worship the Lord of the Assembly. The five-fold worship (*pañcapūjā*) should be performed with the mantra "Laṃ, to the Earth-self," and so forth. Śrī Śiva said:

Śrī Śiva is the Lord of Śrī Śivā; he is the glorious one, worshipped by the Lord of Śrī (Viṣṇu). He is the sprout of auspiciousness, more auspicious than the auspicious, the delight of the virtuous, and the embodiment of the auspicious scriptures (*śivāgama*).

He whose form is unbroken bliss and pure consciousness; who performs the dance of supreme bliss; who places his feet upon the forgetfulness of worldly delusion; who is clothed in animal skins; the mine of compassion.
(2) He who is fond of the speech of Kālī; Time itself; who transcends time; the bearer of all arts and digits; the leader of time; the destroyer of time; the one who sets in motion the wheel of time.

(3) The knower of time; the granter of desires; the beloved; the enemy of desire; the protector of desire; the embodiment of auspiciousness; the lover of the auspicious goddess; the lotus-eyed one. (4)

Kālakaṇṭha (the blue-throated one), Kālakāla (the death of Death), the consumer of the Kālakūṭa poison; the grateful one, the knower of the essence of action, the fire-god, and the dark-brown one. Wearer of an elephant hide as a garment, the bearer of a skull, the remover of impurity; adorned with a garland of skulls, the skeleton, and the destroyer of the Kali age. Dweller on Mount Kailāsa, the Lord of Desire, the poet, free from deceit; the lovely one, whose crest is the moon (Lord of Arts), and the one with a conch-like neck.
Resembling ten million gods of love, he has matted hair and a lotus-like face; he holds the fire of time (*kālāgni*) in his lotus-hand and is as crimson as a *kadamba* flower.
(8) His lotus-hand is adorned with the seal of his own desirable bliss; the sound of his vibrating *ḍamaru* drum has surpassed the roar of the ocean.
(9) He is fierce with a raised *tāṇḍava* dance, a master of the upward *tāṇḍava*, perfected in the leftward *tāṇḍava*, and possesses the majesty of the great *tāṇḍava*. (10)
The great cosmic dance of the dissolution that shatters the shell of the universe; the master of the most fierce *tāṇḍava*; the *tāṇḍava* of whirling motion.

(11) He who loves the dance of Nandin; Nandin; the Lord of Dancers; the wearer of the garb of a river; one who relishes the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of Kālikā’s dance; immovable during the night-dance.
(12) The knower of the measure of Bhṛṅgin’s dance; the performer of a dance resembling a bee; the creator of the world beginning with the ether; the bestower of manifold bliss. (13)

Viṣṇu is free from modification, the Virāṭ, the Lord, and composed of the Virāṭ; he dwells in the lotus-heart of the Virāṭ, the Ordainer (Brahmā), transcending the universe, the all-pervading one. (14) Vīrabhadra, Viśālākṣa, the arrow of Viṣṇu, the lord of the people (Viśāṃpati); the treasury of knowledge, Virūpākṣa, the source of the universe, he whose banner is the bull (Vṛṣadhvaja). (15) The deformed one (Virūpa), pervading all directions, free from sorrow, Virocana; he whose hair is the sky (Vyomakeśa), whose form is the sky, whose shape is the sky, and whose appearance is imperishable. (16)
He who is dear to Vyāghrapāda, who wears a tiger skin, who is the destroyer of disease; he who is the expounder, who is active, who is all-pervading, the witness of the pervaded, and the learned one.

Vyāsa, the destroyer of delusion, whose hands are graced by the gesture of exposition; the bestower of boons, the dwarf, the one worthy of worship, the most excellent, who bears the thunderbolt and the lotus. (18) He who is to be known through the Vedas, whose form is the Veda, the greatest among those who know the Vedas and Vedānta; the knower of the meaning of the Vedas, the source of the Vedas, the limbs of the Vedas, and he who is praised by the Vedas. (19) The beloved of Vaikuṇṭha, the one beyond destruction, whose eyes are like fire; the pervader of all worlds, the prosperous one, who is eternally risen. (20)
Subtler than the subtlest, the Sun, free from both subtlety and grossness; he who wears the daughter of Jahnu (the Gaṅgā) upon his head, the warder-off of birth, old age, and death.
(21) Śūrasena, of auspicious form, of radiant body, with a pure smile; standing nearby, his crown inlaid with priceless jewels.

(22) He whose form is nectar, the presiding lord of the gods, with beautiful eyebrows, whose wealth is happiness, the wise one; the auspicious one, the bestower of auspiciousness, whose vehicle is auspicious, and who is affectionate toward his devotees. (23)

The destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes, the radiant one, the slayer of worldly existence, the treasure-house of devotion, the ruddy one, the refuge, the all-pervading lord, the worthy of shelter, the bestower of happiness, and the auspicious one;
24 The pure one, the supremely generous, the remover of the greatest calamities, the eternal, the existent, the truth, the speaker of truth, and the bestower of prosperity;

25 The wielder of the bow, the lord of wealth, the blessed one, the protector of dharma, the sovereign of the earth, the youthful, the savior, the copper-hued, the one who enables crossing over, and the awakener of reality; 26
The Lord of the Kings of Kings, the Delightful One, the Destroyer of Night-stalkers; He who dwells in the depths, the Lord of the Gaṇas, the Master of the Gaṇas, and He who is devoid of movement.
(27) The Life-Lord of Patañjali, Devoid of the high and the low; the Supreme Self, the Supreme Light, the Most Exalted, and Higher than the highest.
(28) The Man-Lion, the Sovereign of Mountains, the End of Sound, and Devoid of Sound; the Giver of bliss to those who bow, the Worthy of Veneration, whose abode is the King of Mountains. (29)

The divine physician, the knower of all measures, the friend of Brahman, whose nature is Brahman; he who has accomplished what was to be done, the emaciated one, the dark-hued, the bestower of peace, possessing the form of a Śarabha.

(30) The giver of the knowledge of Brahman, the Creator, the one containing the vast embryo, Bṛhaspati; he who is born instantly, worthy of constant worship, the singer of Sāmans, praised by the Sāmans.
(31) The non-terrible one, of wondrous conduct, whose body is bliss, the leader; the Lord of all sciences, the supreme sovereign of all lords. (32)

He whose purpose is everything, who is ever-contented, and who is honored for the meaning of all scriptures; the omniscient one, the giver of all, the immovable pillar, the all-seeing, and he who is fond of battle.
(33) Janārdana, the Lord of the world, the one who wards off birth and karma; the liberator, the destroyer of delusion, the one worthy of joy, and the Great Lord.
(34) The one with plucked-out hair, the pure, Viṣvaksena, the purifier; the thousand-eyed, the thousand-footed, and the one whose faces are thousand lotuses. (35)
The sovereign worshipped by the thousand-eyed Indra, the unifier, the abode of all prosperity; the tawny-hued one of manifold forms, the mighty subduer of strength, the powerful one.
(36) The lord of the mind, accessible to the mind, solely devoted to contemplation; the indifferent witness, attainable through silence, the lord of sages.

(37) Free from pride, the enchanter, devoid of anger, immeasurable, the bestower of honor, the progenitor; the illustrious one, whose self is the sacrificer, the enjoyer of sacrifice, and beloved by those who worship. (38)
The most generous giver, the wearer of the deer-skin, the beloved of Mṛkaṇḍu’s son; invoked by many, the hater of the cities, he who sports within the three cities.

(39) The meritorious one, the Supreme Person, the dweller in the city, the nourisher, the full, the ancient; the recliner, the most auspicious, the peaceful, the ruler, the lover of the dark-complexioned goddess.
(40) The knower of existence, the severer of bonds, transcendent beyond existence, the bestower of fearlessness; the wise one, the lord of men, the destroyer of false convictions. (41)
Untainted, eternally pure, eternally awakened, and free from desire; beyond conceptual construction, without support, changeless, and free from disease.
(42) Unrestrained, without substratum, imperishable, and without end; dwelling in the cave of the heart, transcending the qualities, the embodiment of the Guru, and fond of the cave.

(43) The authority, the sacred syllable Om, the wise one, the giver of life, and the leader of the vital breaths; the soul of the subtle thread, easily attained, translucent, the most excellent, and beautiful-faced. (44)

Adorned with a garland of skulls, he bears a form that brings an end to Time itself. He is difficult to propitiate, unassailable, far removed from the wicked, and hard to approach. (45) He is difficult to comprehend, the destroyer of evil conduct, and the subduer of the intoxicated by pride. He is the Lord of All, the Witness of All, the Soul of All, yet devoid of any witness. (46) He is the one who causes the destruction of all dualities, the warder-off of all calamities, the most beloved of all, and the destroyer of all poverty and suffering. (47)
The Seer, the Revealer, the Tamed One, who bears the form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti; the Destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, the Skillful, the Dweller in the Heart, the Treasure-house of Compassion.
(48) Possessing equal vision, whose desires are truth, praised by the sages Sanaka and others; the Lord, liberated from the five states of death, devoted to the fivefold cosmic functions.
(49) He who loves the five sacrifices, the Imperishable Sovereign of the five vital breaths; the Master of the five elements, whose mind is satisfied by the fivefold worship. (50)
Lord of Obstacles, destroyer of obstacles, with spear in hand, born from the arrow; hidden, most secret, to be protected; protector of cows, progenitor of the Gaṇas.
(51) Of excellent vows, whose resolve is truth, perceivable by oneself, the bringer of happiness; attainable through yoga, established in yoga, bliss of yoga, Yudhiṣṭhira.
(52) Awakening to reality, Lord of reality, the very nature of reality, treasure of austerity; imperishable, three-syllabled, three-eyed, free from partiality. (53)

Worshipped by Māṇibhadra, the venerable one, the master of illusion, the great measurer; bearer of the axe, Lord of the mountain of his lineage, with one lotus-foot slightly bent. (54) King of the Yakṣas, bestower of the fruits of sacrifice, embodiment of sacrifice, the maker of fame; Lord of the Siddhas, progenitor of the Siddhas, the established conclusion, possessing the splendor of the perfected ones.
(55) Abiding in the center of the solar orb, devoid of the quality of passion (rajas); abiding in the center of the fiery orb, most ancient, Lord of Varuṇa. (56)
Abiding in the center of the lunar orb, he is the Moon, the gentle one, the best of friends; he is the Dakṣiṇāgni fire, the Gṛhapati fire, the subduer, and the end of all subduers.

(57) He has four faces, he is the wielder of the discus, he has five faces, and he is the supreme asceticism; he is the abode of the universe, the most excellent, and affectionate toward those who offer salutations. (58) He is the beloved of Gāyatrī, the descendant of Garga, and intent upon blessing the singers; he is of infinite forms, the single Self, the celestial tree, the sacred utterance (Vyāhṛti), and the sacrificial offering (Svadhā). (59)

Vaṭuka is of the form of *svāhā*, possessing a mind full of wealth (*vasumanas*), the protector of the field (*kṣetrapālaka*). He is the one to be heard, the destroyer of enemies, the wielder of the trident, and the ordainer of the Vedas and the Smṛtis.

(60) He is immeasurable, the unrivaled chariot-warrior, Pradyumna, and the Lord of the Pramathas. He is indeed unsurpassed, indifferent, the bestower of liberation, and the one with a joyful countenance. (61) He is the one with uplifted arms, the one whose vital energy flows upwards, and he who is intent on vigorous dancing. He is the master of great illusion, the great devourer, the one of great heroism, and the one with mighty arms. (62)

Great bliss, great shoulders, the great Indra, the great presence; radiant, accessible through meditation, the destroyer of delusive knowledge. (63) The support of the greatness of great supernatural power, the teacher of Mahāsena, the light; the creation that sustains all and grants all boons, situated within the treasure-chest of the hearts of all.
(64) Possessing a long, tawny mass of matted hair, long-armed, sky-clad; the gatherer of all, the lord of self-restraint, the cutter of doubt, the thousand-eyed one. (65)

Free from cause and example, He is the cause who is the birthplace of Heramba; golden and with a beard of gold, He effortlessly fashioned the universe. (66) He is the once-manifested knower, devoid of the extremes of existence and non-existence; established in His own Self, possessing His own weapons, the Lord, non-different from Himself, and the whole universe as His own portion. (67) He is the giver and the gift, the four-footed one, the remover of the bonds of His own Self, and self-existent; the controller, the most excellent, the pervasive, the wielder of the thunderbolt, and the son of Varuṇa. (68)

He is consciousness, the non-duality of consciousness, pure consciousness, and the auspicious lord of consciousness. He is the Infinite (Bhūmā), the Lord of beings, the future, and one who delights in the sacred utterances of Bhūr and Bhuvaḥ.

(69) He is free from the signified and the signifier, the Lord of speech, beyond the reach of words. He is the author of the Vedānta, whose foot is the fourth state (Turya), the lightning-like, and the source of merit.

(70) He is the light that causes the destruction of the inauspicious, for he is not space and is untainted. His desires are fulfilled, he is the permissive witness, his own desire is satisfied; he is indivisible, not minute, and the destroyer (Hara). (71)
Free from attachment and passion, neither short nor long, and without distinctions; independent, possessing pure consciousness, he is to be sought after—he who is unheard and immortal.

(72) He is directly perceptible, without wounds, without marks, free from hatred, an ocean of love; he whose mark is knowledge, the refuge, the knower, accessible through knowledge, and the illuminator.
(73) Resembling a pure, radiant crystal, his majesty is proclaimed by the Vedas; he is the golden-armed commander of the army, the golden-haired lord of the quarters. (74)
Saspiñjara, Paśupati, Tviṣīmat, Adhvanām-pati, Babhluśa, Bhagavat, Bhavya, Vivyādhin, and Vigatajvara;
75 Annānām-pati, Atiyogra, Harikeśa, Advayākṛti, Puṣṭānām-pati, Avyagra, Bhavahetu, and Jagatpati;
76 Ātatāyin, Mahārudra, Kṣetrāṇām-adhipa, Akṣaya, Sūta, Sadasaspati, Sūri, Ahantya, Vanapa, and Vara. 77
Rohita was the chief architect (sthapati), Vṛkṣapati the minister, and Vāṇija the merchant. Kakṣapa, Bhuvanti, and he who was called Bhava were made like water [officers].

Oṣadhīśa was the lord of the virtuous, Uccairghoṣa was Vibhīṣaṇa, and Kṛtsnavīta was the commander of the foot soldiers. Dhāvatsa was the protector of beings (satvapa), Sahamāna was the upholder of truth and dharma, Vivyādhin was Niyama, and Yama was Avyādhipati. Āditya was Kakubha, the knower of time.
Indra is the wielder of the quiver and the bow, the sovereign lord of thieves; he is the one who moves stealthily, the attendant, the wondrous master of the vast forests.

(81) He is the owner of the sacrificial ladle, the lord of those who plunder, the bearer of fifty forms and colors; he is the night-walker, the master of those who cut down, the teacher who roams the mountains.

(82) He is the lord of those who steal by craft, the one who is to be praised, the protector of the desert, and the overlord of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera); he is the one who spreads joy to hundreds, the wise, the lord of the wise, and the divine. (83)
Trāta, Vrātapati, Vipra, Varīyān, Kṣullaka, Kṣamī, Bilmī, Varūthī, Dundubhya, Ahananya, Pramṛśābhidha,
Dhṛṣṇu, Itas, Tīkṣṇadaṃṣṭra, Sudhanvā, Sulabha, Sukhī, Srutya, Pathya, Svatantrastha, Kāṭyonīpya, Karoṭibhṛt,
Sūdyas, Sarasya, Vaiśanta, Nādya, Avadya, Vārṣika, Vaidyutya, Viśada, Medhya, Rōṣmiya, Vāstupa, and Vasu. (84–86)

He who is to be worshipped first in the foremost slaughter; the slayer, the deliverer, the source of joy, the bringer of bliss, the great holy place, the one to be reached by the banks, the one to be reached at the further shore, whose nature is the foot (or the path).

(87) The horned one, the one who carries across, the unobstructed, the one born of foam, the one born of young grass, the one born of the current, the sage, the one to be crossed over, the one to be delighted, the one born of sand, and then the one of fine stones.

(88) Pulastya, the destroyer, the greedy one, the one belonging to the herd, the protector of the cattle, the one born of dry land, the one of green grass, the one to be removed, the one of metal rods, the one of trade, and the source of the powers such as *aṇimā*. (89)
Parṇaśadya, the inward self, serene, supremely exalted; the swiftest, more tranquil than tranquility, bliss, the hero who destroys decay, the imperishable arrow.

(90) The wielder of the noose, the destroyer of sins, the one with sharp arrows, the dispeller of darkness; the bestower of boons and fearlessness, the tail of Brahman, the foremost among the knowers of Brahman.
(91) The teacher of the knowledge of Brahman, the secret one, praised by the Guhyakas; the maker of the end, the support of action, the skillful one, the protector of the wretched. (92)

He is the ninefold essence of liberation from action (*naiṣkarmya*), the Bhairava who dwells in the three cities; he consists of the three measures (*trimātra*) and has the form of the threefold wheel (*trivṛt*); he is the third [state] beyond the three qualities (*triguṇa*).

|| 93 || He is the abode of the three, the cause of the three worlds, the triple agent, moving horizontally and upwards; he is the cessation of phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*), devoid of the duality of name and form. || 94 || He is the Lord of Nature (*prakṛti*), the establisher, the source, the destroyer, and the vast one; he is the one whose purpose is well-ascertained, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), the meaning of the principle of reality (*tatvam*), and composed of austerity (*tapas*). || 95 ||

The benefactor, existing from of old, the intention of all the Upaniṣads; unshackled, the cause of the sky, formidable, with the luster of coral. (96) Indivisible consciousness, the indivisible Self, adorned by a circle of bells; possessing infinite power, the Teacher, abundant, the fulfiller of all.

(97) The conqueror of cities, the primordial one, whose smile is like a flower, the bestower of the fruit of merit; attainable through meditation, the form of the meditator, the object of meditation, the best among those who know the Dharma. (98)

He who is independent yet sovereign, the immovable one, the inner controller, and the performer of a hundred sacrifices; the unchanging, seated upon the tortoise-throne, and the liberator from the seizure of the *kūśmāṇḍa* spirits.
(99) The ocean of compassion that wears away the banks, the auspicious one, the Lord of Kuṅkuma; the wielder of the mace, the master of the Gaṇas, the most venerable, whose weapon is the *tomara*.
(100) The swift one, the support of the universe, Jamadagni, the remover of old age; the wearer of matted locks, the receptacle of nectar, the moon, and the source of nectar. (101)
The most learned, dwelling afar, the repose consisting of pure consciousness; four-armed, possessing a hundred forms, having stilled all curiosity.

(102) The utterance *vauṣaṭ*, the utterance *vaṣaṭ*, the syllable *huṃ*, the skillful maker of *phaṭ*; the one most established in Brahman, the meaning of the sacred thread, the knower of Brahman, whose consciousness is Brahman. (103) The singer, mounted upon Garuḍa, the crusher of the elephant-demon Gajāsura; the proud one, whose abode is the sky, the piercer of the three knots. (104)
The thread of the pearl-string of the elements, the ancient serpent-bearer, the inconceivable boar, the sun, pure existence itself, Sadāśiva;
(105) the one who brings about the descent of power, the capable, the eternal, the treasure-house of blessings, the undigested, the delicate, the other, the seer of the further shore, Purandara;
(106) whose consciousness is unobstructed, the indivisible, the fire, pure consciousness alone, free from passion, cessation, and the refuge of the wise. (107)

Richly adorned with the attire of the clever and the innocent, he transcends the universe and bestows freedom from sorrow. He knows the diversion of the drama of illusion (*māyā-nāṭya*) and is the teacher of the actor of illusion (*māyā-naṭa*).

He is the creator of the drama of illusion, the master of illusion, and the one who releases the machinery of illusion. Free from increase and decrease, he is the light of knowledge and the deceiver of the universe.

He is the devourer of Time (*kāla*), the Lord of Kālī, and adorned by the *Kākeṭika*. Devoid of the six waves of worldly existence, he is the one to be praised and the bestower of the sovereignty of the six divine qualities.

He resides in the six supports, is the principle of Sāṃkhya, and rests upon the six syllables; he is to be pointed out by fire, is to be reached by the wind, is changeless, and possesses unfailing majesty.
Free from both the rejectable and the acceptable, performing the *tāṇḍava* dance with effortless ease; boundless, indefinable, beyond the range of the senses, and the liberator from suffering;
partless, the bliss of the Vedas, yet devoid of worldly joy, and the primordial source; the first-born, the Great Being (*mahābhūta*), whose form is fashioned by His own will;
motionless, the inner bliss, free from blinking, and without interval; awakened, supremely noble, and an ocean of supreme bliss. 112–114.
He is the year complete in its parts, saluted by gods and demons; the giver of liberation, abiding in bliss, free from enmity, and devoid of limiting adjuncts.
He is the radiant one, the supreme reality, the primordial, the auspicious, and the thunderbolt; he whose every volition is utterly stilled, the Lord of the assembly, eternally arisen.

He is liberated from existence and non-existence, whose form is light, who is meditated upon, and who is the sustainer; he who transcends all, who is the most essential essence, accompanied by Ambā, and the bestower of eloquence.

The doer of all, the sustainer of all, consisting of all, the one who takes refuge in sentient beings; the absolute Keśava, the creator of sport, the sole leader. (118) Free from desire and aversion, the wanderer, the increaser of vigor; the destroyer, the fearless, the thirstless, the illuminator.
(119) The ground of rest, the unclothed, the slayer of Han, the purifier; the beloved of heroes, the one whose fear has departed, the destroyer of the pride of the Vindhya mountains. (120)
Delighting in the dance of the *vetāla*, clad in the skin of an elephant, he is one who transgresses all boundaries, playful, and exalted by his valor (121).
He is a treasure-house of dispassion, the enjoyer of the universe, established above all; he is the great creator, the great enjoyer, consisting of pure consciousness, and the Spring (Madhu) (122).
Ungraspable by mind or speech, he has made his abode in the great cavern; free from ego, indivisible, he is a single mass of self-bliss (123).

He dwells within the interior of the world-destroying fire, grasping all that is difficult to grasp; he is the perfected performer of sacrificial sessions, the unifier, and the one endowed with complete majesty.
He who is fully developed, not near, well-considered, and full of longing; he who stands in the assembly, stands in a difficult place, has entered within, and is full of longing;
he who is thoroughly corrupted, well-seated, touched, and the crusher; he who is like a thread, self-luminous, of even character, and always beginning;

he who is established in being, situated in deep sleep, very subtle, and gone to the form of pure existence; he who is free from the arousal of mental constructs, and whose consciousness is equanimous and passionless. (125–127)

He is of the color of the sun, a radiant light, intent upon right vision; he is the abode of the great purport, the certainty of the identity of the inner self and Brahman. (128) He is liberated from the manifestation of the phenomenal world, consisting of direct intuitive perception; he is the impetuous one, whose half-body is the beautiful woman, and who is devoted to dancing. (129) He is the source of yoga, existing as he truly is, and is worshipped by Yakṣas and Gandharvas; he has matted hair, tremulous outer corners of the eyes, and is passionately fond of the great dance. (130)
More brilliant than the rays of the *pāṭala* flower, rooted in the *pārijāta* tree, he is a great sun for the vast forest of sins, possessing the splendor of millions upon millions of suns.
(131) He is as beautiful as ten million gods of love (*kandarpa*), possessing a sweet smile; he is the full moon that fills the waves of the nectar-ocean of dance, the object of merit.

(132) His ornaments consist of garlands made of *rudrākṣa* beads; his radiance is like the glow of white water-lilies (*kalhāra*); on his hand is the bracelet of the lord of serpents, possessing the brilliance of the jewel of immortality (*amṛtamaṇi*).
The sprout of bliss for the eyes of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), white as a jasmine flower; an ocean whose majesty is inaccessible, a treasure-trove of incomparable glory (134);

the sovereign lord of the dancer of consciousness-bliss, who bears a body consisting solely of consciousness; filled with the singular essence of consciousness—He is Śrī Śiva, the illustrious Maheśvara.
Thus ends the Śrī Naṭeśa Sahasranāma Stotra in its entirety.

To the left is the Daughter of the Mountain (Pārvatī), and in front is the King of Bulls (Śiva); behind is the Sage Jaimini, and on both sides are the illustrious Vyāsa and Patañjali; and in the intermediate directions starting from the northwest are the sacrificers dwelling exclusively in Tillavaṇa, along with Brahmā and the other gods; yet in the center of this city of the lotus-like heart, the Lord of the Golden Assembly reigns in triumph.
May this be offered to the illustrious Naṭeśa.
May there be auspiciousness.
The Five Jewels of Śrī Naṭeśa.
From the illustrious Naṭarāja, the King of Dancers, the Lord of Knowledge, who is exultant in bestowing manifold auspiciousness,
whose face is as beautiful as the full moon, and who is crowned by the king of stars;
I know no reality whatsoever beyond Bharga;
[I bow] to him whose hand is adorned by the *ḍakka* drum, whose throat is blue with poison,
whose eyes are like full-blown lotuses, and who is worshipped by the king of serpents.
From Śambhu, whose feet are worshipped by the tiger-footed one (Vyāghrapāda) and whose toes are curled by Śiva,
I know no supreme reality whatsoever.
